advances: Actual polytopal mixed fibers and a supplied marked boundary martingale. The reduced law is an intrinsic volume transport with equal mass and affine moments. Deriving a new reduced boundary stress or a bound from original bulk cap budgets requires additional input.

proof:
The canonical hull lies in $C$ and includes all sampled fibers, so its integer fibers agree with $C$. Its base projection is $\operatorname{conv}P$, whose integer points are exactly $P$ because the original projection contains it. Every generating point satisfies the common affine support inequality, and every exposed $u$-face of a sampled fiber lies on its equality plane. Thus $F_u$ projects onto $\operatorname{conv}P$, and its fiber at $p$ is exactly the $u$-exposed face of $K_p$.

On a full-dimensional polytope, the exposed $u$-face is either a facet, whose relative interior has unique normal $u$ and whose relative boundary is $\mathcal H^{d-1}$-null, or a lower-dimensional face of zero own-boundary measure. For an interval it is the appropriate endpoint with the corresponding signed normal. In all cases a regular point with mark $u$ lies on the exposed face, so restriction to $F_u$ equals restriction to the mark $u$ for $\eta$, and also for $\nu$ by absolute continuity. Because $\Pi$ preserves the mark, the rows with input in $F_u$ stay in $F_u$, and the rows with output in $F_u$ have input there. The restricted rows therefore have both full restricted marginals and preserve their conditional means.

When $\operatorname{aff}P=\mathbb R^n$, the canonical hull is full-dimensional because it has full base projection and a full-dimensional continuous fiber. Positive sector mass supplies a $(d-1)$-dimensional vertical exposed face, and the full projection of $F_u$ supplies $n$ independent base directions. The equality plane has dimension $n+d-1$, so $F_u$ is a facet. The supporting-facet reduction of [d374ad317ca7547f](../facts/d374ad317ca7547f.md) now applies to $C_0$ with its base coefficient $-a$ and with incoming correction zero, as just proved. In particular the ambient area factor $\sqrt{1+\lVert a\rVert^2}$ and its reciprocal base projection coarea factor are separate from the mixed fiber measure. The target and transport identity hold even with deficient base rank because $\Psi$ fixes $p$ and is an isometry on every continuous fiber, and its affine inverse preserves the restricted barycentric rows. Finitely many reduced fibers of dimension at most $d-1$, at least one of dimension $d-1$, give the asserted intrinsic Hausdorff measure. Density pullback composes each allocation with $\Psi$, and direct substitution into the cap inequality gives the displayed sign and constant. The same substitution applies to pure-base, whole-space, and empty traces.

For the last assertions, group the generating points in a hull representation of $(z,x)$ by base. For each choice of the base weights $\theta_p$, the attainable $x$ form the Minkowski combination $\sum_p\theta_pK_p$. Its support in each unit direction $u$ is $\sum_p\theta_p h_{K_p}(u)$, which depends only on $z$ by the sampled affinity. Equality of support functions makes all combinations at $z$ the same body. This also shows $h_{(C_0)_z}(u)=a(u)\cdot z+b(u)$ for every real base in the hull.

There are finitely many positive normal sectors because the sampled fibers are finitely many polytopes. Apply the first part on each sector to decompose $\Pi$. Under full base span, a nonvertical facet exposed by $c\cdot z+v\cdot x=\beta$, $v\ne0$, lies in $F_u$ with $u=v/\lVert v\rVert$, since a point on it maximizes $u\cdot x$ within its own fiber. Its points also satisfy $(c+\lVert v\rVert a(u))\cdot z=\beta-\lVert v\rVert b(u)$. If the base coefficient is nonzero, this imposes a second independent hyperplane equation and contradicts the dimension of a facet. Thus the coefficient vanishes, and nonemptiness gives equality of the two supporting planes and faces. Each projects onto the full base hull. A normal determines its affine interpolation uniquely on the spanning sample, hence determines the facet. At a regular measured fiber point the only possible continuous normal of an owning facet is its mark, and the positive mark sectors already supply such a facet almost everywhere.

The use of the canonical hull matters with only sampled support. For example, the hull of $\{0,1\}\times[-1,1]$ and $(1/2,2)$ has upper sampled support $1$ at both integer bases, while $x\le1$ fails at the unsampled point. Affine support on every real base of $C$ would give the corresponding support plane of $C$ directly.

statement:
Let $C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d$ be a compact convex body, $d\ge1$, and let $P$ be all its nonempty integer bases. Assume $P\ne\varnothing$ and all its fibers $K_p$ are full-dimensional compact polytopes in $\mathbb R^d$. Write $C_0=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{p\in P}(\{p\}\times K_p)$, and let $\eta$ be the sum of the own-fiber $\mathcal H^{d-1}$ boundary measures with the regular continuous outward unit normal marked. Suppose a finite source $\nu\ll\eta$ is coupled to $\eta$ by a physical martingale $\Pi$ preserving this mark.

Fix a unit vector $u$ and suppose $h_{K_p}(u)=a\cdot p+b$ for every $p\in P$. The plane $u\cdot x-a\cdot z=b$ supports $C_0$. Write $F_u$ for its exposed face and assume $\eta(F_u)>0$. The restrictions of $\eta$ and $\nu$ to $F_u$ are their entire normal-$u$ sectors up to null sets. There are zero crossings in both directions for $\Pi$, so $\nu(F_u)=\eta(F_u)$, and the restricted rows couple $\nu|_{F_u}$ to the full target $\eta|_{F_u}$.

For a linear isometry $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to u^\perp$, set $\Psi(z,t)=(z,Et+(a\cdot z+b)u)$ and $D=\Psi^{-1}(F_u)$. The pulled-back target is $\mu_u=\sum_{p\in P}\mathcal H^{d-1}|_{D_p}$, the intrinsic Hausdorff measure of the reduced trace, and $\widehat\nu_u=(\Psi^{-1})_\#(\nu|_{F_u})\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\mu_u$ with equal mass and affine physical moments. The measure identity includes zero-weight smaller faces and uses endpoint counting when $d=1$. If $\operatorname{aff}P=\mathbb R^n$, $F_u$ is a nonvertical supporting facet and $D$ is a full-dimensional polytope in $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$. If $d\nu=\sum_j\lambda_j\alpha_j\,d\eta$ is an actual cap-allocation law, its reduced density is $\sum_j\lambda_j(\alpha_j\circ\Psi)$. A cap $c_j\cdot z+v_j\cdot x\ge\beta_j$ restricts to
$$
(c_j+(v_j\cdot u)a)\cdot z+(E^{\mathsf T}v_j)\cdot t
\ge \beta_j-(v_j\cdot u)b,
$$
with the original allocation on coincident positive-measure boundaries and indicator agreement almost everywhere for null equality loci.

If the sampled support is affine in the base for every unit direction, the canonical fiber at every $z=\sum_p\theta_p p$ in $\operatorname{conv}P$ is the Minkowski combination $\sum_p\theta_pK_p$, independently of the representation. The boundary coupling decomposes into finitely many such unweighted-target volume transports. With full base span, each nonvertical facet is the common support face $F_u$ for its continuous unit normal $u$, projects onto all of $\operatorname{conv}P$, and has a different continuous unit normal from every other nonvertical facet. Almost every measured own-fiber boundary point then has a unique nonvertical facet owner.
title: Affine sampled support closes a marked normal sector
